ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants were asked to report how much they felt sympathetic, soft-hearted, warm, compassionate and caring towards themselves during the prior MDMA session.

> For instance, unlike more inner-directed psychedelic-assisted therapy approaches (Alpert et al., 2026), the treatment manual included an 'Empathic Reimagining Task' during either MDMA dosing or integration sessions, wherein participants were guided through bringing a compassionate, warm perspective to a memory characterized by high shame, self-criticism, or perceived social rejection.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

While social anxiety disorder is defined by fear of scrutiny from others (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), a strained relationship with the self may lie at its heart (Cox et al., 2004; Gregory & Peters, 2017).

text.text: Cognitive models delineate that people with heightened social anxiety often deem aspects of themselves as deficient, flawed, or contrary to societal standards (Moscovitch, 2009).

text.text: This negative self-perception renders social interactions as threats-chances for flaws to be exposed and negative evaluation, failure, or rejection to ensue (Afram & Kashdan, 2015; Buckner et al., 2010).

text.text: Viewing social situations through a self-critical lens, people with social anxiety may avoid social encounters, ruminate on perceived missteps, inhibit authentic self-expression, and discount positive feedback (Blackie & Kocovski, 2018; Hofmann, 2007; Plasencia et al., 2016).

text.text: 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) is a psychoactive compound that has broad-acting effects, increasing the release of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine, alongside circulating levels of oxytocin and vasopressin.

text.text: In sum, self-compassion may be a valuable therapeutic resource for addressing the maintenance factors of social anxiety disorder, and a small though growing body of work has evaluated psychological mechanisms of action within psychedelic-assisted therapy and suggests that self-compassion is a promising potential mechanism of change within psychedelic-assisted therapy and MDMA-AT.

We propose that self-compassion serves as an important process of change in MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder (Luoma & Lear, 2021), especially when the psychotherapy component of MDMA-AT is optimized to target underlying cognitive and behavioral processes theorized to maintain social anxiety disorder (e.g., harsh self-criticism), as in the current intervention (Luoma et al., in press).

In this paper, we assess the role of self-compassion in a MDMA-AT iteratively developed to synergistically pair the effects of therapy with psychedelics, and target underlying social anxiety disorder processes.

This study represents a secondary data analysis of a randomized waitlist, delayedtreatment control trial of MDMA-AT for 20 adults with social anxiety disorder (NCT05138068; (Lear et al., 2023).

text.text: Overall, throughout treatment, therapists aimed to foster strong therapeutic rapport, a sense of psychological safety, and supported clients in both receiving care from others and cultivating self-compassion by modeling warmth, authenticity and nonjudgment.
The treatment initially followed an inner-directed framework, guided by the MDMA-AT manual for PTSD developed by Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelics Studies (Mithoefer, 2017).

text.text: The treatment is grounded in the conceptualization of social anxiety disorder as a shame-centered condition, in which self-protective behaviors are driven by a central belief that the authentic self is fundamentally flawed.
These behaviors paradoxically maintain social anxiety and prevent the corrective interpersonal experiences necessary for change.
As such, the therapy encourages behavioral changes that allow for expectancy violations and new learning, and compassionate reframing of shame-based schemas.
For instance, during preparation sessions, participants' histories of social experiences of shame and criticism were explored and reframed through a compassionate lens.

Dosing sessions included structured tasks such as guided reprocessing of shame-related memories and "Authenticity Experiments" in which clients engaged in commonly avoided interpersonal behaviors with the therapist team.

Integration sessions often incorporated a perspectivetaking exercise, the Empathic Reimagining Task, which guides clients to revisit shame-laden memories from a compassionate vantage point accessed during dosing.

Between sessions, clients are supported in practicing values-consistent interpersonal behavior that may otherwise be avoided, with support from the therapist team on navigating these new experiences with self-compassion.
Midomafetamine (commonly referred to as MDMA), an investigational product not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, was supplied by Resilient Pharmaceuticals Inc.
Initial doses were 80 mg and 120 mg, respectively, and a 40 mg supplemental dose in most cases.
Further dosing information is available in (Lear et al., 2023).

text.text: Specifically, for (c), we fit a 3-phase time model: time 1 ('preparation phase', i.e., the three preparatory sessions), time 2 ('post-dose 1 phase', i.e., the two integration sessions after MDMA dose 1), and time 3 ('post-dose 2 phase', i.e., the two integration sessions after dose 1 as well as the post-treatment assessment).
Another tested model comprised two phases: time 1 (preparation phase), and time 2 (i.e., the remaining sessions following the first dosing session).
Model (c) was selected (with time coded per three intervention phases) and used a random intercept and slope terms based on model fit statistics (AIC, BIC, log likelihood).
Robust standard errors were used to account for heteroscedasticity.

To examine whether state self-compassion experienced during each of the two MDMA sessions was associated with changes in trait self-compassion, we initially specified a multilevel model with state self-compassion predicting the change in trait self-compassion from before to after the dosing session, with MDMA dose (1 vs. 2) included as a withinperson factor, and a random intercept for participant.
However, the model fit was singular, indicating that the random-effects structure was not supported by the data.

Accordingly, we ran two separate simple linear regressions examining whether: (1) state self-compassion during dose 1 was associated with the change in trait self-compassion between phase 2 and phase 1; and (2) state self-compassion during dose 2 was associated with the change in trait self-compassion between phase 3 and phase 2.
Model assumptions were evaluated via diagnostic plots, and robust standard errors were applied to address heteroskedasticity.
No covariates were included in the models.

text.text: Overall, these findings suggest that our MDMA-AT intervention tailored to target core cognitive and behavioral social anxiety disorder processes was associated with changes in self-compassion: the intervention fostered high self-compassion levels during the two dosing sessions and trait-level increases in self-compassion following the MDMA dosing sessions.

Both greater state self-compassion during dosing sessions and greater overall trait self-compassion changes across the intervention appear to hold therapeutic value for certain outcomes within MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder, especially internalized shame.

Trait self-compassion significantly increased over the course of MDMA-AT, with a large-sized effect, consistent with observed increases in self-compassion following psychedelic use in past research (Domínguez-Clavé et al., 2022; van der Kolk et al., 2024).

text.text: A nonlinear pattern of change best fit the data, wherein self-compassion increased in a stepwise fashion immediately after each dosing session.
The largest increase occurred from preparation to post-dose 1, with additional gains post-dose 2.

However, individual selfcompassion change trajectories across MDMA-AT were highly variable, suggesting that this observed pattern of change was not uniformly experienced across participants and that there may be multiple pathways through which self-compassion may develop.

Participants generally reported experiencing high levels of state self-compassion during MDMA dosing sessions, consistent with descriptions of heightened self-compassion in prior qualitative work of psychedelic-assisted therapy (Agin-Liebes et al., 2025; Barone et al., 2019).

text.text: The most reliable associations overall were between self-compassion and internalized shame.

We observed that greater self-compassion, whether state changes measured during dosing sessions or trait changes self-compassion in subsequent sessions, were associated with reductions in internalized shame.

Other outcomes were associated with either state or trait self-compassion: greater state self-compassion was associated with depressive symptom reductions, while trait self-compassion increase was associated with reductions in feelings of thwarted belonging.

Although sample size precluded formal mediation analysis and led to limited power to detect statistical significance, these findings contribute to a growing body of work suggesting that state self-compassion (Agin-Liebes et al., 2025) and trait selfcompassion (Zeifman et al., 2025) may serve as important mechanisms of change for certain core psychosocial outcomes within psychedelic-assisted therapy.

text.text: Speculatively, intense, acute experiences of self-compassion may be more impactful for internalized shame and depressive symptoms than for social anxiety, functional impairment, and sense of belonging because these outcomes may be more directly rooted in negative internal processes that could be interrupted by self-compassion experiences.

In contrast, social anxiety and belonging may depend more heavily on social factors and interpersonal learning, in addition to negative internal processes, thus making the connection between self-compassion and these outcomes weaker and less direct.

Our findings with state self-compassion are partially consistent with past research. Zeifman et al., (2025) similarly found that state self-compassion mediated the relationship between treatment (psilocybin vs. placebo) and depressive severity and suicidal ideation for participants (n = 59) with major depressive disorder.

text.text: The discrepancy between our results and this prior research may be due to population (social anxiety disorder vs. major depressive disorder), analysis (sample size precluded formal mediation analysis in the current study), substance type (MDMA vs.
psilocybin), therapy type (an evidence-based adaptation of psychotherapy for psychedelicassisted therapy vs. nondirective psychological support) or ceiling effects in the present study.

For instance, state self-compassion was generally high during MDMA sessions, with few participants scoring below the scale's midpoint (none in session 1, and two in session 2); such ceiling effects may have limited variability and reduced the ability to detect associations with several outcomes, such as social anxiety, functioning, or belonging.

Inconsistent with our hypothesis, state self-compassion experienced during dosing sessions had small, nonsignificant associations with increases in trait self-compassion from before to after the dosing sessions.

This suggests that the cultivation of trait-level selfcompassion may not depend solely on the intensity of in-session self-compassion experiences, but also on unfolding processes outside of peak in-session experiences (e.g., integration sessions, reflection, repeated practice in daily life).
Alternatively, the noted ceiling effects for state self-compassion during dosing sessions may have limited their statistical associations.

Our results were partially consistent with our hypotheses: trait self-compassion changes had statistically significant associations with certain beneficial outcomes (reduced internalized shame and thwarted belonging), but not others (social anxiety symptoms, functional impairment and depressive symptoms).

Speculatively, the constructs of internalized shame and belonging map most closely onto the constructs measured by the SCS-SF and were thus most directly influenced by changes in self-compassion over the course of MDMA-AT.

For instance, a greater sense of common humanity (vs. isolation), may have contributed to less thwarted belonging, while greater self-kindness (vs. harsh selfcriticism), may have diminished self-shaming.
In contrast, social anxiety, functional impairment and depressive symptoms may operate more distally from the construct of trait self-compassion.
Changes in self-compassion may thus influence these outcomes less strongly, directly, or immediately.

For instance, it may take a longer period for changes in self-compassion to translate into durable decreases in depressive symptoms, whereas the impacts of trait self-compassion on shame may be noticeable immediately.
Later increases in self-compassion, occurring after the second MDMA dosing session, were associated with benefits, whereas earlier increases, occurring after the first dosing session, were not.
This pattern of findings could simply reflect a measurement artifact: variables assessed more proximally to outcomes may have stronger associations with outcomes.
Alternatively, this pattern may speak to clinically relevant temporal dynamics.

For instance, the therapeutic effects of self-compassion may accumulate over the course of treatment, such that later or sustained increases confer greater benefit than initial trait selfcompassion changes.
If replicated, this would suggest the value of additional dosing sessions or self-compassion interventions to reinforce early gains in self-compassion changes.
Another possibility is that changes in trait self-compassion require time to consolidate before they translate into broader psychological benefits.
Early self-compassion increases may represent an emerging way of relating to oneself that takes time to apply to daily life before meaningful changes in shame and sense of belonging become evident.

Our results are somewhat inconsistent with prior work-while we also found that trait self-compassion changes conferred benefit, Agin-Liebes et al., (2025) found support for the mediating role of trait self-compassion on PTSD and depressive symptoms in MDMA-AT for PTSD, whereas in our study, self-compassion changes were not significantly associated with mental health symptoms (depression or social anxiety symptoms).
However, comparison of our findings with prior work is made difficult by several methodological differences, including analysis method, clinical population (social anxiety disorder vs.
PTSD), therapy type (cognitive-behavioral theory-driven vs. inner-directed) and the modest sample size and power of the current study.
Future research in larger samples is needed to examine what outcomes trait self-compassion changes may mediate, over what timescale, and in what samples.

While we did not form a priori hypotheses around the role of baseline selfcompassion on outcomes, we included baseline levels of trait self-compassion in our models and observed a consistent pattern: greater self-compassion levels during the preparation period were associated with several improvements: less post-treatment social anxiety, functional impairment, internalized shame, and thwarted belonging.

Potentially, greater baseline trait self-compassion may facilitate greater engagement with and thus benefit from treatment, such as through increasing openness to MDMA experiences, persistence with behavioral experiments, psychological flexibility, or ability to disengage from anticipatory anxiety or post-event rumination.

This observed pattern suggests that initial self-compassion levels may serve as a moderator of certain outcomes in MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder, though this should be directly tested in future larger trials.
Further, if replicated, the generalizability of this pattern to other outcomes and clinical populations should be examined.

Preliminary support for self-compassion's role in MDMA-AT in the current study may reflect features of the specific study design, rather than being generalizable to MDMA-AT in other contexts/for other disorders.
Indeed, the psychotherapy component of the treatment was carefully and iteratively developed and included elements that aimed to enhance MDMA's effect on self-compassion.

For instance, unlike more inner-directed psychedelic-assisted therapy approaches (Alpert et al., 2026), the treatment manual included an 'Empathic Reimagining Task' during either MDMA dosing or integration sessions, wherein participants were guided through bringing a compassionate, warm perspective to a memory characterized by high shame, self-criticism, or perceived social rejection.

text.text: This intervention component, distinct from MDMA's effect, might explain the degree of change in self-compassion over the course of treatment, and some of the patterns of associations between self-compassion and outcome described here.

Future work would benefit from examining whether the observed findings generalize to other types of MDMA-AT and psychedelic-assisted therapy, and whether adding therapeutic techniques specifically involving self-compassion enhance outcomes within MDMA-AT and psychedelic-assisted therapy.
Furthermore, future work would benefit from replicating this work in larger more demographically heterogeneous samples.
Several additional limitations should be considered.
First, because this was an openlabel trial, causality cannot be inferred.

Second, the small sample size introduces instability in effect size estimates and measures of variability and significantly lowers statistical power; null findings in particular should be interpreted with caution.

Third, our method of examining changes in trait self-compassion across treatment phases may oversimplify change; future studies with larger samples could employ more flexible longitudinal modeling approaches to better characterize nonlinear dynamics and examine if different trajectories predict different outcomes or if there are diverse trajectories that predict similar outcomes.
Additionally, future work may benefit from identifying predictors of these trajectories, including baseline characteristics, in-session experiences, and integration processes.

MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder appears capable of fostering both acute state self-compassion and enduring trait-level self-compassion changes.
Both trait self-compassion changes over the course of MDMA-AT and state self-compassion experienced during MDMA dosing sessions contributed to certain beneficial psychosocial outcomes.

While state self-compassion was most robustly associated with improvements in depressive symptoms and internalized shame, trait self-compassion changes were most robustly associated with improvements in internalized shame and sense of belonging.

Both acute state self-compassion experiences and trait self-compassion changes over the course of treatment may serve as distinct mechanism of change within MDMA-AT; future work should examine whether these patterns generalize in larger mechanistically-oriented psychedelic-assisted therapy trials, with other types of psychotherapy, and whether findings are transdiagnostic or specific to certain clinical populations.
